explanation: Pressure = normal force per unit area (P = F/A).

subtopic: Pressure on small versus large area same force
questionText: Same force applied. Which produces greater pressure?
explanation: P = F/A. Smaller A → larger P (e.g., sharp knife vs blunt).

questionText: At depth h in a liquid of density ρ, pressure due to liquid = :
explanation: Hydrostatic pressure P = ρgh (above atmospheric).

questionText: A hydraulic system multiplies force because:

options.a: Pressure is the same throughout fluid (Pascal's principle)

explanation: Pascal's principle: pressure transmitted equally → small force × small area = large force × large area.

questionText: Standard atmospheric pressure is approximately:
explanation: Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted by the weight of air above a unit area. At sea level, standard atmospheric pressure is approximately 101,325 Pa (Pascal), or 101.3 kPa, or 1 atm. It decreases with increasing altitude because there is less air above.

questionText: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of:
explanation: Mercury barometer = atmospheric pressure supports Hg column (~760 mm Hg).

subtopic: Newton first law inertia rest uniform motion
questionText: A passenger in a car lurches forward when brakes are applied suddenly. This demonstrates:
explanation: Body continues moving forward at original speed (inertia) → first law.

questionText: Which type of friction must be overcome before an object starts moving?
explanation: Static friction = force needed to start motion. Once moving, kinetic friction (lower).

questionText: Stopping distance of a car depends on:

options.a: Initial speed (∝ v²) and braking distance

explanation: Stopping d = thinking d + braking d. Braking d ∝ v² (kinetic energy).

questionText: At terminal velocity, a falling object has:
explanation: Terminal velocity = constant velocity when drag force = weight (Newton's 1st law).

questionText: When a force is perpendicular to displacement, the work done is:
explanation: W = F × s × cos θ. When θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0 → W = 0.

questionText: When a skydiver reaches terminal velocity, which is correct?
explanation: Terminal velocity = constant speed → a = 0 (Newton's 1st). Drag = weight.

questionText: A car starts at 10 m/s and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 5 seconds. Using average velocity, find the distance travelled.
A 1000 kg car needs to accelerate at 2.5 m/s². Net force required =:
What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph give?
explanation: Gradient of v-t graph = Δv/Δt = acceleration.

questionText: Newton's 2nd law gives the definition of newton as:
explanation: 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s². SI unit of force.

questionText: Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude because:

options.a: Less air above at higher altitudes

explanation: Higher altitude = less air column above = less weight pushing down = lower P.

questionText: What is the pressure 10 m below the water surface? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²)
At constant temperature, gas pressure and volume obey:
explanation: Boyle's law: P × V = constant at constant temperature.

questionText: A gas at 200 kPa occupies 100 mL. If pressure is increased to 400 kPa (constant T), new volume =:
explanation: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → 200×100 = 400×V₂ → V₂ = 50 mL.

questionText: At constant pressure, gas volume is proportional to:
explanation: Charles' law: V/T = constant (T in kelvin).

questionText: At constant volume, gas pressure is proportional to:
explanation: Pressure law (Gay-Lussac): P/T = constant (T in kelvin).

questionText: Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on an object equals:
explanation: Buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced by object.

subtopic: Floating condition object denser less dense
questionText: An object floats in water when:

options.b: Object's weight is more than water displaced

explanation: Floats: object density < fluid density → buoyant force ≥ weight.

questionText: An object sinks in water when:
explanation: Sinks: object density > fluid density → weight > buoyant force.

questionText: A 0.5 m³ object is fully submerged in water. Buoyant force = (ρ_w 1000 kg/m³, g = 10)
How does a hydraulic press lift a heavy load?

options.a: Small force × small piston = larger force × larger piston (Pascal)

explanation: Pascal's principle: pressure transmitted equally → small F₁ produces large F₂.

questionText: A hydraulic press has piston areas 10 cm² and 100 cm². If 50 N is applied on small piston, force on large piston = :

subtopic: Pressure exerted shoe heel versus flat
questionText: Why does a sharp heel produce more pressure than a flat sole (same force)?

options.a: Smaller contact area → higher pressure (P = F/A)

explanation: Smaller A → higher P (P = F/A). Sharp heel sinks into ground.

questionText: A mercury barometer at sea level reads approximately:
explanation: Standard atmospheric pressure supports 760 mm Hg column at sea level.

questionText: Pulling the plunger of a sealed syringe (gas trapped) decreases gas volume; pressure:
explanation: V decreases → P must increase to keep P×V constant (Boyle's law).

questionText: A submarine adjusts its depth by controlling:

options.a: Buoyancy by changing mass of water in ballast tanks

explanation: Submarine changes overall density (fills/empties ballast tanks with water) to dive/surface.

questionText: Hot air balloons rise because:

options.a: Hot air is less dense than cool surrounding air → buoyancy

explanation: Heating air decreases its density; if overall density < surrounding air → buoyant force up.

questionText: Density is defined as:
explanation: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance: ρ = m / V (kg/m^3 or g/cm^3). Substances with higher density sink in substances of lower density (e.g., iron sinks in water). Water has density 1,000 kg/m^3 at 4 degreesC.

questionText: An object of mass 100 g and volume 200 cm³ density is:

subtopic: Ideal gas equation PV equals nRT
questionText: The ideal gas law is:
explanation: PV = nRT (combines Boyle, Charles, Avogadro; R = 8.31 J/(mol·K)).

questionText: A pressure gauge on a gas cylinder reads absolute pressure when:

options.a: Calibrated with reference to vacuum (0 Pa)

explanation: Absolute P = gauge reading + atmospheric. Gauge P is relative to atm.

questionText: A small piston of area 20 cm² has gas at 100 kPa. Force on piston =:

subtopic: Liquid pressure same depth different shape
questionText: Liquid pressure at the same depth depends on:
explanation: Hydrostatic paradox: P = ρgh depends only on depth, not vessel shape.

questionText: Who invented the mercury barometer?
explanation: Torricelli invented the mercury barometer in 1643.

questionText: An object floats higher in a denser fluid. This is because:

options.a: Denser fluid provides more buoyant force per volume displaced

explanation: Larger ρ → larger buoyant force at same displaced volume → floats higher.

subtopic: Specific heat capacity calculation Q = mcΔT
questionText: How much heat is needed to raise 2 kg of water by 10°C? (c = 4200 J/(kg·°C))

subtopic: Specific latent heat of fusion melting ice calculation
questionText: How much heat is needed to melt 2 kg of ice at 0°C? (Lf = 334,000 J/kg)

subtopic: Specific latent heat of vaporisation boiling water
questionText: How much heat is needed to vaporise 1 kg of water at 100°C? (Lv = 2,260,000 J/kg)

subtopic: Latent heat temperature constant during melting
questionText: During melting, the temperature of ice:

options.a: Remains constant until all melted (heat = latent)

explanation: During phase change, temperature stays constant; all heat goes to latent heat (no T change).

subtopic: Boyle's law cooler warming syringe expansion
questionText: A gas in a sealed container is cooled. At constant volume, pressure:
explanation: P/T = constant (in Kelvin). Lower T → lower P.

subtopic: Brownian motion evidence for kinetic theory
questionText: Brownian motion provides evidence for:
explanation: Random motion of suspended particles (e.g., pollen) shows molecular motion of fluid.

subtopic: Kinetic theory of gases basic assumption
questionText: The kinetic theory of gases assumes that gas particles:

options.a: Are in continuous random motion; collisions elastic

explanation: Kinetic theory: gas particles random motion, elastic collisions, no forces between particles (ideal).

questionText: Gas temperature is proportional to the average:
explanation: T (K) ∝ average KE of particles (translational motion).

questionText: In a fluid being heated from below, convection occurs because hot fluid:
explanation: Hot fluid = less dense → buoyancy → rises. Cool fluid replaces → convection current.

subtopic: Land sea breeze day time direction
questionText: During daytime, sea breeze blows from:

options.a: Sea to land (cool air from sea)

explanation: Day: land heats faster, hot air rises → cool sea air flows in (sea breeze).

questionText: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium when:
explanation: Thermal equilibrium = same T; no net heat flow between them (zeroth law).

questionText: In metallic solids, conduction occurs mainly by:
explanation: Metals: free (delocalised) electrons vibrate + travel, transferring heat energy quickly.

questionText: All objects (above absolute zero) emit:
explanation: All objects with T > 0 K emit EM radiation (mostly IR). Higher T → more + shorter λ emission.

subtopic: Vacuum flask design minimise heat transfer
questionText: Why does a vacuum flask (thermos) keep hot liquid hot AND cold liquid cold?

options.a: Double wall with vacuum between reduces conduction + convection; silvered surfaces reduce radiation

explanation: Vacuum (no medium) eliminates conduction/convection. Silvered surfaces reflect IR radiation.

questionText: Specific latent heat of fusion is the heat needed to:

options.a: Change 1 kg of solid to liquid at constant temperature

explanation: Latent heat of fusion = heat to change 1 kg solid → liquid (no T change).

questionText: Heat capacity of a substance is:

options.a: Heat needed to raise temperature by 1°C (J/°C)

explanation: Heat capacity C = Q/ΔT (units J/°C or J/K).

subtopic: Specific heat capacity substance value comparison
questionText: Which substance has the highest specific heat capacity among common substances?
explanation: Water has unusually high SHC (4200 J/kg·°C) due to H-bonds; useful as coolant and heat reservoir.

questionText: Compared to boiling, evaporation generally occurs:

options.a: At temperatures below boiling point (surface only)

explanation: Evaporation = surface only, any T below bp. Boiling = throughout, at bp (with bubbles).

questionText: Which method of heat transfer does NOT require a medium?
explanation: Radiation = EM waves; travels through vacuum (e.g., Sun to Earth).

questionText: A bimetallic strip in a thermostat uses two metals that:
explanation: Two metals with different expansion rates → strip bends on heating → opens/closes switch.

questionText: In a refrigerator, the refrigerant absorbs heat during:
explanation: Refrigerant evaporates in fridge coils → absorbs latent heat → cools interior.

subtopic: Latent heat release effect candle wax solidifying
questionText: A burning candle's wax melt drips and then solidifies. During solidification, the wax:
explanation: Solidifying = liquid → solid releases latent heat to environment.

subtopic: Latent heat large with no temperature change
questionText: Why does boiling water stay at 100°C while being heated?

options.a: All heat goes to latent heat of vaporisation (no temp rise)

explanation: At boiling, all added heat goes to Lv (breaking intermolecular bonds), not raising T.

questionText: On a hot day, sprinkling water on the floor cools it because:

options.a: Water evaporates, absorbing latent heat from surroundings

explanation: Water evaporates → absorbs Lv (cooling effect) → cools floor/air.

subtopic: Why ice-cold water in thermos melts slower
questionText: A thermos flask keeps ice from melting quickly because vacuum:
explanation: Vacuum = no medium → no conduction/convection. Silvered walls reflect IR → minimal heat gain.

questionText: Specific heat capacity c of a substance is the heat needed to:

options.a: Raise 1 kg of substance by 1°C (or 1 K)

explanation: c = Q/(m·ΔT). Units J/(kg·°C) or J/(kg·K).

questionText: Convection does NOT occur in:
explanation: Convection requires fluid (liquid or gas) — particles free to move. Solid particles vibrate in fixed positions.

questionText: Which material is best as an insulator to prevent heat flow?
explanation: Fibreglass traps air (poor conductor) → good insulator.

subtopic: Convection in oven heating circulates air
questionText: Convection currents in an oven circulate heat by:

options.a: Hot air rising; cool air sinking

explanation: Conventional oven: heating element warms air at bottom → hot air rises → cool air falls → circulation.

questionText: The Kelvin scale is considered absolute because:

options.a: 0 K is the lowest possible temperature (no molecular motion)

explanation: 0 K = absolute zero = no thermal motion (theoretical). T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.

subtopic: Snell's law calculation n sin θ calculation
questionText: Light travels from air into glass. n(glass) = 1.5, sin θ₁ = 0.5 in air. Find sin θ₂.
explanation: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ → 1×0.5 = 1.5×sin θ₂ → sin θ₂ = 0.333.

questionText: Refractive index (n) of a medium is defined as:

options.a: Speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed in medium (c/v)
options.b: Speed of light in medium ÷ c (v/c)

explanation: n = c/v (always > 1 for any medium denser than vacuum).

questionText: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from:

options.a: Denser to less dense medium AND beyond critical angle

explanation: TIR needs: denser → less dense (e.g., glass → air) + angle > critical angle.

subtopic: Critical angle calculation n sin c equals 1
questionText: For glass n = 1.5, critical angle (from glass to air) ≈ :

subtopic: Optical fibre application total internal reflection
questionText: How does light travel along an optical fibre?

options.a: By total internal reflection at the core-cladding interface

explanation: Fibre: core (high n) + cladding (lower n); light hits core-cladding at angle > critical → TIR → guided.

subtopic: Convex lens converging image real inverted
questionText: A convex lens forms an image that is real, inverted, and magnified when object is placed:
explanation: Object between f and 2f → real, inverted, magnified image (beyond 2f).

questionText: An object is 20 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Image distance =:
explanation: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u (sign convention). Or simply: v = u·f/(u-f) = 20·10/(20-10) = 20 cm.

questionText: Concave lens always produces what type of image?
explanation: Diverging lens = always virtual, upright, smaller image on same side.

questionText: A magnifying glass is a convex lens used when the object is placed:

options.a: Within the focal length (between lens and f)

explanation: Magnifying glass: object within f → virtual, upright, magnified image (for inspection).

questionText: An object of height 5 cm forms an image of height 10 cm using a lens. Magnification =:
explanation: Magnification M = image height / object height = 10/5 = 2. (Also M = -v/u.)

subtopic: Light refraction cause speed change medium
questionText: Light refracts when it crosses a boundary because:

options.a: Its speed changes in different media

explanation: Refraction = light speed changes in different media → wavelength changes → bending.

subtopic: Electromagnetic spectrum order radio to gamma
questionText: Which is the correct order of EM spectrum from longest to shortest wavelength?

options.a: Radio > microwave > infrared > visible > ultraviolet > X-ray > gamma
options.b: Gamma > X-ray > UV > visible > IR > microwave > radio

explanation: Longest λ to shortest: radio, microwave, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma rays.

subtopic: Speed of light in vacuum constant c
questionText: Speed of light in vacuum is approximately:
The wavelength range of visible light is approximately:
explanation: Visible light: 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red).

questionText: What happens when white light passes through a prism?

options.a: It is dispersed into a spectrum of seven colours
options.b: It is reflected back as white light
options.c: It is absorbed completely with no transmission
options.d: It is converted entirely into heat energy

explanation: A prism disperses white light into its component colours (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet) because different wavelengths refract by different amounts. This is known as dispersion and is caused by each colour bending at a slightly different angle.

questionText: When white light passes through a triangular glass prism, what optical phenomenon occurs?

options.a: Dispersion into a spectrum of seven colours
options.b: Total internal reflection back to source
options.c: Complete absorption with no light emerging
options.d: Conversion of light into electrical current directly

explanation: A triangular glass prism disperses white light into its constituent colours (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet) because each wavelength refracts at a slightly different angle. This is known as dispersion, first studied by Isaac Newton. Total internal reflection requires specific conditions; absorption would prevent light from emerging.

questionText: A camera forms an image on the film/sensor that is:
explanation: Camera lens (convex) produces real, inverted, smaller image on sensor for object beyond 2f.

questionText: What does a prism do to white light?
explanation: Prism = dispersion (refractive index varies with λ) → separate colours into spectrum.

questionText: Two convex lenses have focal lengths 5 cm and 20 cm. The 5 cm lens has:
explanation: Lens power P = 1/f (in metres). P(5 cm) = 1/0.05 = 20 D; P(20 cm) = 5 D. Shorter f = more powerful.

subtopic: Prism spectrum red less bent violet more
questionText: Through a prism, red light is bent less than violet because:

options.a: Red has longer wavelength → smaller refractive index

explanation: Red (longer λ) → smaller n → less refraction → less bending. Violet → more bending.

questionText: What sequence of colours makes up a rainbow (in order, top to bottom)?

options.a: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (ROYGBIV)

explanation: Spectrum order: ROYGBIV (longest λ, red, outermost).

subtopic: Total internal reflection critical angle formula
questionText: The relationship for critical angle is:
explanation: sin(c) = 1/n where n is refractive index of denser medium.

questionText: Snell's law relates angles of incidence and refraction to:

options.a: Refractive indices of the two media

explanation: Snell's Law describes refraction: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where n is the refractive index of the medium and θ is the angle from the normal. When light passes from a less dense medium (lower n) to a denser medium (higher n), it bends towards the normal.

questionText: Lens power is measured in:
explanation: Lens power P = 1/f (m) = dioptres. Shorter focal length = higher power.

questionText: How does the human eye focus on objects at different distances?

options.a: By changing the shape of the lens (accommodation)

explanation: Ciliary muscles change lens shape → focal length changes → light focuses on retina.

questionText: Calculate resistance: 12 V across 4 A.
explanation: Ohm's Law states that the current I flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage V across it, with the constant of proportionality being 1/R, where R is the resistance. Formula: V = I x R, where V is in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms.

questionText: Two resistors (5 Ω and 10 Ω) in series total =:
explanation: Series: R_total = R₁ + R₂ = 5 + 10 = 15 Ω.

questionText: Two 10 Ω resistors in parallel total resistance =:
An electric kettle runs at 240 V and draws 8 A. Power =:
A 2 kW kettle used for 3 hours consumes:
explanation: Electrical energy consumed E = P x t (in watt-hours or kilowatt-hours). 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10⁶ J = 1 unit on the electricity bill. Cost = Energy (kWh) x rate per unit. For example, a 100 W bulb running 10 hours uses 1 kWh of energy.

questionText: Calculate heat dissipated per second in a 10 Ω resistor with 2 A current.
explanation: Electrical power dissipated in a resistor can be calculated using P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R. For a 10 Ω resistor with 2 A current flowing through it: P = I^2R = 4 x 10 = 40 W. This electrical energy is converted to heat (Joule heating).

subtopic: Magnet field lines north to south
questionText: Outside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines go from:
explanation: Outside magnet: field lines emerge from N, return to S (in closed loops).

subtopic: Magnet like poles repel unlike attract
questionText: Two north poles of bar magnets held close to each other will:
explanation: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

subtopic: Magnetic field strength around current wire
questionText: A long straight wire carrying current produces a magnetic field that:

options.a: Forms concentric circles around the wire (right-hand grip rule)
options.b: Forms straight lines parallel to wire

explanation: Right-hand grip rule: thumb = current direction; fingers curl = field direction (concentric circles).

subtopic: Solenoid magnetic field bar magnet equivalent
questionText: A solenoid carrying current acts like:

options.a: A bar magnet (with N and S poles depending on current direction)

explanation: Solenoid = electromagnet; field similar to bar magnet (N at one end, S at other).

questionText: Electromagnetic induction was discovered by:
explanation: Faraday (1831) discovered electromagnetic induction (changing magnetic flux induces EMF).

questionText: For electromagnetic induction to occur, the magnetic flux through a coil must:

options.a: Change (change in B, area, or angle)

explanation: Changing flux = changing magnetic field × area × cos θ. Induced EMF requires dΦ/dt ≠ 0.

questionText: Lenz's law states that the direction of induced current:

options.a: Opposes the change that produced it

explanation: Lenz's law = induced current creates magnetic field opposing the original flux change.

questionText: An AC generator is based on:

options.a: Electromagnetic induction (rotating coil in magnetic field)

explanation: AC generator: coil rotates in magnetic field → flux changes → EMF induced → alternating current.

questionText: Three resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in series. What is the total resistance of the circuit?
explanation: For resistors in series, the total resistance is the sum: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 4 + 6 + 12 = 22 Ω. In series, the same current flows through each resistor, and the voltage divides across them.

questionText: Which of the following best describes how an electromagnet is made?

options.a: By wrapping a coil of insulated wire around a soft iron core and passing a direct current through it
options.b: By hammering a steel bar while it is heated until red hot
options.c: By stroking a piece of soft iron repeatedly with a bar magnet in the same direction
options.d: By placing a permanent magnet inside a hollow plastic tube

explanation: An electromagnet consists of a coil of insulated wire (solenoid) wrapped around a soft iron core. When current flows through the coil, the iron becomes magnetised. Switching off the current removes the magnetism, making it a temporary magnet (unlike a permanent magnet).

subtopic: DC motor principle current in field
questionText: A DC motor works because:

options.a: Current in coil in magnetic field experiences force (turning effect)

explanation: F = BIL; current in coil in B-field → force on each side → couple/rotation (motor effect).

questionText: A fuse wire is rated '5 A'. This means:

options.a: It melts when current exceeds 5 A (protecting circuit)

explanation: Fuse melts if current > rating → opens circuit → protects appliances/wiring.

subtopic: Live neutral earth wire colours in plug
questionText: Which colour indicates the earth wire in a Malaysian 3-pin mains plug?
explanation: Earth wire = yellow-green stripes. Live = brown. Neutral = blue (Malaysia standard).

subtopic: Live wire brown colour UK Malaysia
questionText: The live wire colour in modern Malaysian mains plug wiring is:
explanation: Brown = live (L), Blue = neutral (N), Green/yellow stripes = earth (E).

subtopic: Double insulation symbol no earth needed
questionText: Why do some appliances have a 'double insulation' symbol and no earth wire?

options.a: Internal + external insulation prevents user contact with live parts

explanation: Double insulation = two layers; even if one fails, second protects. No earth needed.

subtopic: Power transmission high voltage reduce loss
questionText: Why is electrical power transmitted at high voltage over long distances?

options.a: Lower current reduces I²R power loss in cables
options.b: High voltage is cheaper to make

explanation: P_loss = I²R; high V → low I → less heat loss in cables. Transformers step up at generation.

questionText: A loudspeaker operates on the principle of:

options.a: Current-carrying coil in magnetic field experiencing force (vibrates cone)

explanation: Coil attached to cone in magnetic field → AC current → varying force → vibration → sound.

questionText: Using the right-hand grip rule for a solenoid, fingers curl in the direction of:
explanation: Right-hand grip: fingers curl = current direction; thumb points = N pole / field direction.

questionText: Why does Lenz's law demonstrate conservation of energy?

options.a: Without opposition, induced current would create free energy (impossible)

explanation: If Lenz's law didn't hold (no opposition), mechanical work → electric energy would violate conservation.

questionText: Which is a hard magnetic material suitable for permanent magnets?
explanation: Steel = hard magnetic material (high retentivity); keeps magnetisation. Soft iron = temporary magnet.

questionText: In a DC motor, 'back EMF' opposes the applied voltage. This results in:

options.a: Lower current after initial surge (limiting current)

explanation: Spinning motor generates back EMF → opposes supply → reduces current draw (limits heat).

subtopic: National grid transformer step down use
questionText: Before electricity enters homes, transformers are used to:

options.a: Step down high voltage to safe 240V household supply

explanation: Step-down transformers near homes reduce transmission voltage (e.g., 11 kV) to 240V.

questionText: Fleming's left-hand rule shows direction of:

options.a: Force on current-carrying conductor in magnetic field (motor effect)

explanation: Left-hand rule: First finger = Field (B), Second finger = Current (I), Thumb = Force/motion (F).

questionText: Fleming's right-hand rule shows direction of:

options.a: Induced current in a moving conductor (generator effect)

explanation: Right-hand rule: First finger = Field (B), Thumb = Motion (v), Second finger = Induced current.

subtopic: Diode allows current one direction only
questionText: What does a diode do in a circuit?

options.a: Allows current in one direction only

explanation: Diode = one-way valve for current (forward biased = conducts; reverse biased = blocks).

questionText: In a simple electric motor, what is the function of the split-ring commutator?

options.a: It reverses the direction of current in the coil every half-turn so the coil rotates continuously
options.b: It increases the magnetic field strength of the permanent magnets
options.c: It converts alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) for the household supply
options.d: It measures the voltage produced across the rotating coil

explanation: The split-ring commutator in a DC motor reverses the current direction in the coil every half turn. This ensures that the torque on the coil always acts in the same rotational direction, allowing continuous rotation instead of oscillation.

questionText: A NOT gate (inverter) has what logic function?
explanation: NOT gate = inverter. Input 0 → output 1; input 1 → output 0.

questionText: For an AND gate with inputs A=1 and B=1, output =:
explanation: AND: output 1 only if all inputs 1. (1,1) → 1.

questionText: For an OR gate, when is output 1?

options.a: When ANY input is 1 (at least one)

explanation: OR: output 1 if any input is 1 (1 OR 0 = 1; 0 OR 0 = 0).

questionText: Where is most of the mass of an atom concentrated?
explanation: Nucleus contains protons + neutrons → >99.9% of atom's mass (electrons negligible).

questionText: Which particle has a positive charge?
explanation: Proton = +1 charge. Neutron = 0. Electron = −1.

subtopic: Atomic notation A and Z meaning
questionText: In the notation ²³⁵₉₂U, the numbers mean:

options.a: Mass number 235 = p + n; atomic number 92 = protons

explanation: A (top) = mass number (p+n). Z (bottom) = atomic number (protons = electrons in neutral atom).

questionText: How is the carbon-14 isotope written?
explanation: ¹⁴₆C: A = 14 (6p + 8n), Z = 6 (6 protons = carbon).

questionText: Which of the following is a fossil fuel commonly used for generating electricity in power stations?
explanation: Coal is a fossil fuel formed from the remains of ancient plants compressed over millions of years. Other fossil fuels include petroleum (oil) and natural gas. Solar, wind and geothermal are renewable energy sources (not fossil fuels).

questionText: What is an alpha particle?
explanation: α particle = ⁴₂He²⁺ nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons).

questionText: What is a beta particle (β⁻)?

options.a: A high-speed electron emitted from nucleus (neutron → proton + electron)

explanation: β⁻ = electron. Neutron converts → proton + electron (+ antineutrino).

questionText: What is a gamma ray (γ)?
explanation: γ = high-energy photon (EM radiation, no mass, no charge), often accompanies α/β decay.

subtopic: Alpha decay change in atomic number
questionText: In α (alpha) decay, the atomic number (Z) changes by:
explanation: α decay loses 2 protons → Z reduces by 2; A reduces by 4.

questionText: In β⁻ (beta-minus) decay, the atomic number (Z) changes by:
explanation: β⁻ decay: neutron → proton + e⁻. So Z (protons) increases by 1. A unchanged.

questionText: In a nuclear power station, the energy released during nuclear fission comes primarily from:

options.a: Conversion of a small amount of mass into a large amount of energy (E=mc^2)
options.b: Combustion of uranium with oxygen releasing heat
options.c: Burning of coal mixed with radioactive uranium ore
options.d: Chemical reaction between U-235 atoms and water

explanation: Nuclear fission of uranium-235 (or plutonium-239) splits the nucleus into smaller fragments, releasing energy according to Einstein's mass-energy equation E=mc^2. A tiny amount of mass is converted into a huge amount of energy (heat), which boils water to drive turbines.

questionText: Which of the following is an advantage of using solar energy compared to fossil fuels?

options.a: Solar energy is renewable and does not produce carbon dioxide during operation
options.b: Solar energy is cheaper to install than coal-fired power plants
options.c: Solar energy can generate electricity 24 hours a day regardless of weather
options.d: Solar panels are made entirely from non-metallic materials

explanation: Solar energy is a renewable resource (sunlight is essentially inexhaustible on human timescales) and generates electricity without emitting CO₂ (a greenhouse gas) during operation. Fossil fuels release CO₂ when burned, contributing to climate change.

questionText: Carbon-14 dating is used to determine:
explanation: C-14 dating: organic materials up to 50,000 years old. Rocks use K-Ar or U-Pb dating.

questionText: How is carbon-14 produced naturally in the atmosphere?

options.a: Cosmic rays collide with nitrogen → C-14 in upper atmosphere

explanation: Cosmic ray neutrons + N-14 → C-14 + proton. C-14 enters biosphere via CO₂ uptake.

subtopic: Nuclear fission heavy nucleus split uranium
questionText: Nuclear fission involves:

options.a: Splitting of a heavy nucleus into smaller fragments + energy

explanation: Fission: heavy nucleus (e.g., U-235) absorbs neutron → splits into lighter fragments + energy + more neutrons.

subtopic: Nuclear fusion light nuclei join helium
questionText: Nuclear fusion occurs when:

options.a: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus + energy

explanation: Fusion: light nuclei combine (e.g., hydrogen → helium in Sun) → releases huge energy.

questionText: In a nuclear chain reaction, the role of neutrons is to:
explanation: Each fission releases neutrons → which cause more fission → chain reaction (controlled = reactor).

subtopic: Nuclear reactor control rods boron cadmium
questionText: Control rods in a nuclear reactor absorb excess neutrons to:
explanation: Control rods (boron, cadmium) absorb neutrons → moderate chain reaction → prevent runaway.

questionText: What is the role of a moderator in a nuclear reactor?

options.a: Slow down fast neutrons to increase fission efficiency

explanation: Moderator (graphite, water) slows fast neutrons → thermal neutrons → better fission probability.

questionText: Which is NOT a source of background radiation?
explanation: Background radiation: cosmic rays, terrestrial (radon), food, medical. Not mobile phones (ionising vs non-ionising).

questionText: Iodine-131 is used in medicine to:
explanation: I-131 concentrates in thyroid → diagnosis/treatment of thyroid disorders (Goitre, cancer).

questionText: Americium-241 in smoke detectors works by:

options.a: Ionising smoke particles to detect fire

explanation: Am-241 ionises air in chamber → current flows. Smoke disrupts → alarm triggered.

questionText: The Sun's energy comes mainly from:

options.a: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen to helium in its core

explanation: Sun: proton-proton chain → 4 H → He + energy (millions of kelvin required).

questionText: A film badge worn by radiation workers measures:
explanation: Film badge = personal dosimeter; photographic film darkens with radiation exposure → dose measured.

questionText: Which of the following best describes the function of a control rod in a nuclear reactor?

options.a: To absorb excess neutrons and slow down or stop the nuclear chain reaction
options.b: To reflect neutrons back into the reactor core to increase efficiency
options.c: To convert heat energy from fission directly into electrical energy
options.d: To filter radioactive waste products from the coolant water

explanation: Control rods (typically made of boron or cadmium) absorb neutrons in a nuclear reactor. By lowering or raising the rods, the operator controls the rate of the chain reaction. Fully inserted rods stop the reaction (used for shutdown).

subtopic: Solar system planets order from sun
questionText: What is the correct order of planets from the sun in our solar system?

options.a: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune

explanation: Mercury → Venus → Earth → Mars → Jupiter → Saturn → Uranus → Neptune (from sun).

subtopic: Planet Earth unique liquid water life
questionText: Why is Earth able to support life (unlike other planets)?

options.a: Liquid water, suitable temperature range, atmosphere with oxygen

explanation: Earth: liquid water, moderate T (habitable zone), O₂ atmosphere → supports life.

subtopic: Sun source of energy nuclear fusion hydrogen
questionText: What is the main source of the Sun's energy?

options.a: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium

explanation: Sun: proton-proton fusion → 4H → He + 2e⁺ + 2ν + energy (E = mc²).

questionText: In which atmospheric layer does weather occur?
explanation: Troposphere = lowest layer (~0-12 km); contains weather, clouds, water vapour.

questionText: Why is the ozone layer important?

options.a: Absorbs harmful UV radiation from sun

explanation: Ozone (O₃) in stratosphere absorbs UV-B and UV-C → protects life from harmful radiation.

questionText: What causes most earthquakes?

options.a: Movement of tectonic plates at boundaries

explanation: Earthquakes = sudden release of stress at plate boundaries (fault lines).

questionText: Most volcanoes form at:
explanation: Most volcanoes = subduction zones + divergent boundaries (mid-ocean ridges).

questionText: Who proposed the idea of continental drift and Pangaea?
explanation: Wegener (1912): continents once joined as 'Pangaea' and have drifted apart.

subtopic: Earth magnetic field protects solar wind
questionText: How does Earth's magnetic field protect life?

options.a: Deflects harmful solar charged particles (solar wind)

explanation: Magnetosphere deflects solar wind charged particles → protects atmosphere from being stripped.

subtopic: Compass needle north Earth magnetic pole
questionText: A compass needle points north because:

options.a: Earth is a giant magnet (compass aligns with field)

explanation: Compass = small magnet; aligns with Earth's magnetic field (towards magnetic north).

questionText: Which gas is the main contributor to the greenhouse effect?
explanation: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour trap infrared → greenhouse effect → global warming.

questionText: What causes day and night on Earth?

options.a: Earth's rotation on its axis (24 hours)

explanation: Earth rotates on its axis every 24 h → day (facing sun) and night (facing away).

questionText: What causes seasons on Earth?

options.a: Earth's axis tilt (23.5°) combined with revolution around sun

explanation: Tilted axis + revolution → varying sun angle and day length → seasons.

questionText: What primarily causes ocean tides?

options.a: Gravitational pull of Moon on Earth (mostly)

explanation: Moon's gravity pulls ocean water → 2 bulges (high tides); Earth rotates → 2 high/low tides/day.

subtopic: Spring tide alignment new full moon
questionText: When do spring tides occur?

options.a: New moon and full moon (Sun, Moon, Earth aligned)

explanation: Spring tides = new/full Moon (Sun + Moon gravity aligned → strongest tides).

questionText: When do neap tides occur?

options.a: First and third quarter moons (Sun/Moon at right angles)

explanation: Neap tides = first/third quarter moons (Sun vs Moon gravity partially cancel).

questionText: Galileo discovered 4 moons orbiting which planet?
explanation: Galileo (1610) discovered 4 largest moons of Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto).

subtopic: Asteroid belt location between Mars Jupiter
questionText: The asteroid belt is located between:
explanation: Asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter orbits (remnants of planet formation).

questionText: What does one light-year measure?

options.a: Distance light travels in one year (~9.46 × 10¹² km)

explanation: 1 light-year = distance light travels in 1 year ≈ 9.46 × 10¹² km (used for astronomy).

subtopic: Star life cycle main sequence sun
questionText: Our Sun is currently in which stage of its life cycle?
explanation: Sun = main sequence star (H fuses to He). Will become red giant in ~5 billion years.

subtopic: Big Bang theory universe expansion origin
questionText: The Big Bang theory explains:

options.a: Origin and expansion of the universe ~13.8 billion years ago

explanation: Big Bang: universe began as extremely dense/hot point ~13.8 Ga, expanding ever since.

questionText: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram plots:
explanation: H-R diagram: stars classified by luminosity (y-axis) and temperature (x-axis).

subtopic: Red shift galaxy expanding universe Hubble
questionText: What does red-shift of distant galaxies indicate?
explanation: Redshift = wavelength increases → galaxies moving away → universe expanding (Hubble's law).

questionText: Why are some telescopes (like Hubble) placed in orbit instead of ground?

options.a: Avoid atmospheric distortion; clearer space images

explanation: Above atmosphere → no air turbulence → sharper images; access to UV/IR blocked by atmosphere.

questionText: The angle of tilt of Earth's rotational axis is approximately:
explanation: Earth's axial tilt = 23.5° → causes seasons.

subtopic: Greenhouse effect carbon dioxide global warming
questionText: How does increasing atmospheric CO₂ contribute to global warming?

options.a: CO₂ traps infrared radiation from Earth surface

explanation: Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) absorb IR → trap heat → global warming.

questionText: Solar cells (photovoltaic panels) work by:

options.a: Converting sunlight directly to electricity using semiconductor
options.b: Converting light to heat to boil water

explanation: PV cells: photons knock electrons free in semiconductor (e.g., Si) → direct current electricity.

subtopic: Wind energy turbine kinetic to electrical
questionText: How does a wind turbine generate electricity?

options.a: Wind spins blades → kinetic energy rotates generator

explanation: Wind KE → rotating blades → shaft turns generator → electricity (electromagnetic induction).

questionText: Tidal energy is generated by:

options.a: Using tidal water flow to drive turbines

explanation: Tidal power: rising/falling tides drive turbines in barrage → renewable electricity.

questionText: Which of these is NOT a fossil fuel?
explanation: Fossil fuels: coal, oil (petroleum), natural gas. Wood is biomass (renewable resource).

questionText: Why are fossil fuels considered contributors to climate change?
explanation: Combustion of fossil fuels (CxHy) + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O → increases atmospheric CO₂.

questionText: In a typical water treatment plant, which is the correct order of steps?
explanation: Water treatment: sedimentation (settle), filtration (filter), chlorination (disinfect), supply.

questionText: Why is chlorine added to drinking water?
explanation: Chlorination = disinfection; Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO → HClO kills microbes.

questionText: Which is a primary benefit of recycling?

options.a: Reduces landfill use; conserves natural resources

explanation: Recycling reduces waste in landfill + saves raw materials + energy.

subtopic: Three Rs hierarchy reduce reuse recycle
questionText: What is the correct order of the 3Rs (most preferred to least)?
explanation: Most preferred = reduce (use less), then reuse, then recycle (last resort).

questionText: Your 'carbon footprint' refers to:

options.a: Total greenhouse gases emitted by your daily activities
options.c: The weight of carbon in your body

explanation: Carbon footprint = total CO₂-equivalent emissions from lifestyle (transport, food, energy).

questionText: Penicillin works by:

options.a: Disrupting bacterial cell wall synthesis (kills bacteria)

explanation: Penicillin inhibits cell wall formation → bacteria cannot survive → infection cleared.

questionText: How does a vaccine provide immunity?

options.a: Stimulates immune system to produce antibodies + memory cells

explanation: Vaccine = weakened/inactivated pathogen → triggers immune response → antibody production + memory.

questionText: In bread-making, yeast causes dough to rise by:

options.a: Producing CO₂ gas during fermentation (anaerobic respiration)

explanation: Yeast: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (anaerobic fermentation). CO₂ makes dough rise.

questionText: In a food chain, which organism is always at the start (base)?
explanation: Producers (autotrophs, green plants) form base of food chain via photosynthesis.

questionText: A food web differs from a food chain because:

options.a: It shows multiple interconnected food chains in an ecosystem

explanation: Food web = many interconnected food chains → more realistic ecosystem representation.

questionText: Approximately what percentage of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next in a food chain?
explanation: Only ~10% of energy transfers up each trophic level; rest lost as heat/movement/waste.

questionText: An example of an endangered species in Malaysia is:
explanation: Malayan tiger is critically endangered (small wild population). Specific conservation focus in Malaysia.

questionText: How does deforestation affect biodiversity?

options.a: Destroys habitats → species lose homes → extinction risk

explanation: Habitat destruction = main cause of biodiversity loss; species can't migrate or adapt quickly.

subtopic: Air pollution primary gas carbon monoxide vehicle
questionText: Which gas is a major pollutant from car exhausts causing health problems?
explanation: CO from incomplete combustion → binds haemoglobin (200x affinity of O₂) → suffocation.

questionText: Why is carbon monoxide (CO) toxic to humans?

options.a: Binds haemoglobin strongly, prevents O₂ transport in blood

explanation: CO + Hb → COHb (carboxyhaemoglobin); prevents O₂ binding → tissue hypoxia → death (high exposure).

questionText: Excess nutrients (fertiliser) in water cause:
explanation: Nutrients + warm water + light → algal bloom → decomposition uses O₂ → fish die (eutrophication).

questionText: Why are some pesticides (e.g., DDT) considered persistent organic pollutants?

options.a: They do not break down easily; accumulate in food chains (bioaccumulation)
options.c: They are only toxic to plants

explanation: POPs = persistent (long-lasting), bioaccumulative (build up in fatty tissues), toxic. DDT famous example.

questionText: In the carbon cycle, which process returns CO₂ to the atmosphere?
explanation: Respiration by all organisms returns CO₂. Combustion of fossil fuels also adds CO₂.

questionText: In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis removes CO₂ from atmosphere by:

options.a: Converting CO₂ + H₂O into glucose + O₂ (using sunlight)

explanation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (light energy captured by chlorophyll).

questionText: Which food products are produced using fermentation by microorganisms?
explanation: Fermentation by bacteria/yeast → yoghurt, cheese, bread, soy sauce, vinegar, alcohol.

questionText: Ethanol biofuel can be produced by:
explanation: Fermentation of sugarcane/maize by yeast → ethanol → blended with petrol (gasohol).

questionText: Nanotechnology involves structures at the scale of:
explanation: Nano = 10⁻⁹ m. Nanoparticles, nanotubes have unique properties at this scale.

questionText: How is insulin for diabetes produced by biotechnology?

options.a: Insert human insulin gene into bacteria; bacteria produce insulin

explanation: Recombinant DNA technology: human insulin gene → plasmid → E. coli → produces pure insulin.

questionText: One benefit of a pest-resistant genetically modified crop is:
explanation: GM pest-resistant crops = less pesticide spray + less crop loss → higher yield, environmental benefit.

subtopic: Acid rain effect on aquatic ecosystems
questionText: How does acid rain affect aquatic ecosystems?

options.a: Lowers lake pH; harms fish/amphibians; disrupts food web

explanation: Acid rain (NOₓ, SO₂ → HNO₃, H₂SO₄) drops to water → acidic → fish eggs/species die.

questionText: Why does eutrophication eventually kill fish?

options.a: Algae bloom blocks light + decomposition uses dissolved O₂; fish suffocate
options.b: Fish eat algae and get sick

explanation: Algae cover → less light → plants die → bacteria decompose them → deplete O₂ → fish suffocate.

subtopic: Sustainable development basic triple bottom line
questionText: Sustainable development aims to balance:

options.a: Economic growth, environmental protection, social well-being

explanation: Sustainability = meeting present needs without compromising future generations (3 pillars).

subtopic: Catalytic converter vehicle exhaust pollution reduction
questionText: How does a catalytic converter reduce car exhaust pollution?

options.a: Converts harmful gases (CO, NOₓ) to less harmful (CO₂, N₂, H₂O)

explanation: Catalytic converter: catalysts (Pt, Pd, Rh) speed up oxidation/reduction of pollutants to harmless gases.

subtopic: Carbon monoxide haemoglobin treatment fresh air
questionText: First-aid treatment for CO poisoning includes:

options.a: Move to fresh air, seek medical attention, possibly oxygen

explanation: Move victim to fresh air → oxygen therapy → hospital. CO has 200x affinity for Hb.

questionText: Why is tetraethyl lead (TEL) no longer added to most petrol?

options.a: Toxic to humans; damages catalytic converters; cause lead pollution

explanation: TEL (leaded petrol) = toxic, neurotoxic, ruins catalytic converters → phased out globally.

subtopic: Water filter ceramic versus activated carbon chlorine
questionText: Which method does NOT purify drinking water?

options.a: Adding chlorine is needed only for disinfection

explanation: Standing water does NOT purify - just settles particles. Boiling, filtration, chlorination all purify.

questionText: How does plastic pollution in oceans affect marine wildlife?

options.a: Animals ingest plastic; become entangled; can die

explanation: Sea turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish → eat; seals entangled in plastic rings → injury/death.

questionText: Why are heavy metals like mercury considered serious pollutants?
explanation: Heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd) = persistent, bioaccumulative, toxic → biomagnification up food chains.

questionText: What is biological magnification (biomagnification)?

options.a: Toxin concentration increases up the food chain

explanation: Biomagnification: persistent toxin (e.g., DDT) accumulates → higher concentration in predators at top.

questionText: How did CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) damage the ozone layer?

options.a: CFC releases Cl atoms; Cl catalyses O₃ destruction

explanation: CFC + UV → Cl· + other; Cl· + O₃ → ClO + O₂; ClO + O → Cl· + O₂ (chain).

subtopic: Montreal Protocol CFC ban international treaty
questionText: The Montreal Protocol (1987) addressed which environmental issue?
explanation: Montreal Protocol = international treaty to phase out CFCs/ozone-depleting substances.

questionText: Why are fossil fuels called non-renewable?

options.a: They take millions of years to form; cannot be replaced once used

explanation: Non-renewable = used faster than formed (millions of years for fossil fuels; rate of use depletes reserves).

questionText: Renewable resources are those that:

options.a: Can be replenished naturally within a human lifetime
options.b: Never run out regardless of use

explanation: Renewable = replaced by natural processes faster than consumed (e.g., solar, wind, biomass, hydropower).

questionText: An ethical concern of genetic engineering is:

options.a: Potential misuse, designer babies, modified ecosystems

explanation: Ethical concerns: GM impact on ecosystems, biodiversity loss, access inequality, 'designer babies' ethics.

questionText: What is a biodegradable material?

options.a: Material that decomposes naturally by microorganisms

explanation: Biodegradable = broken down by bacteria/fungi naturally (e.g., paper, food waste, some bioplastics).

questionText: In sewage treatment, the secondary stage uses:

options.a: Bacteria to break down organic matter (biological filter)

explanation: Secondary treatment: aerobic bacteria decompose organic matter in activated sludge/trickling filters.

questionText: Composting kitchen waste is an example of:
explanation: Composting = biological decomposition of organic waste → nutrient-rich soil amendment.

questionText: Which is an example of green technology in everyday life?
explanation: Solar panels = renewable energy generation = green technology example.

questionText: What is a 'carbon offset'?

options.a: Compensating for emissions by funding projects that reduce/remove CO₂

explanation: Carbon offset = paying for emissions reduction elsewhere (e.g., tree planting, renewable projects).

subtopic: Lead petrol effect children cognitive impairment
questionText: Lead (Pb) in petrol causes health problems including:

options.a: Cognitive impairment in children; nervous system damage

explanation: Pb is neurotoxic: damages developing brains in children → lower IQ, behavioural issues.

questionText: How does light pollution affect nocturnal wildlife?
explanation: Artificial light disorients nocturnal animals (insects, birds, sea turtles) → disrupts ecosystems.

questionText: Noise pollution affects wildlife by:
explanation: Anthropogenic noise interferes with animal calls (mating, predator detection) → ecological harm.

questionText: What is the purpose of an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)?

options.a: To evaluate potential environmental damage before development

explanation: EIA = study to predict + assess environmental effects before project approval (e.g., new highway, factory).

questionText: Which action best demonstrates a 'green consumer' choice?

options.b: Always buying cheapest regardless of packaging

explanation: Green consumer = chooses eco-friendly products, reusable, less packaged, local/sustainable.

subtopic: Lysosome Tay Sachs disease lipid storage
questionText: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by deficiency of a specific enzyme in:
explanation: Tay-Sachs = lysosomal hexosaminidase A deficiency → lipid accumulation → neurodegeneration.

questionText: Which pattern of inheritance suggests mitochondrial DNA mutation?

options.a: Only affected children of affected mothers (not fathers)

explanation: Mitochondrial inheritance = mother only (sperm mitochondria destroyed).

questionText: An example of a polygenic (many-gene) trait in humans is:
explanation: Polygenic traits (height, skin colour, IQ) = many genes + environment.

subtopic: Pleiotropy single gene multiple traits example
questionText: Pleiotropy describes:
explanation: Pleiotropy = one gene → multiple phenotypic effects (e.g., sickle cell = anaemia + resistance to malaria).

subtopic: Codon degeneracy multiple codons same amino acid
questionText: Why is the genetic code said to be 'degenerate'?

options.a: Multiple codons can code for the same amino acid
options.b: Each amino acid has only one codon
options.c: Each codon codes for multiple amino acids

explanation: Degenerate = 64 codons, only 20 amino acids; multiple codons per aa (e.g., UUU & UUC = Phe).

questionText: What is a null hypothesis (H₀) in a scientific experiment?

options.a: Statement of no effect/no difference to be tested

explanation: Null H₀ = no significant effect/difference. Alternative Hₐ = there IS an effect.

questionText: In an experiment investigating how light affects plant height, what is the dependent variable?
explanation: Dependent variable = measured outcome (height). Independent = manipulated (light). Controlled = kept same.

questionText: Why is repeating an experiment (replication) important?

options.a: Confirms reliability; reduces random error chance

explanation: Replication = verify results are reliable + not due to chance.

questionText: Standard deviation measures:

options.a: The average spread of data around the mean

explanation: Standard deviation σ = measure of dispersion around mean. Larger σ = wider spread.

questionText: Reliable measurements are those that:
explanation: Reliable = consistent/reproducible. Valid = measure what intended.

questionText: An experiment is valid if it:

options.a: Tests what it claims to test (no confounding variables)

explanation: Validity = accurate measurement of intended variable; controls confounders.

questionText: What is a histogram useful for showing?
explanation: Histogram = bars touching, for continuous data (intervals).

questionText: Which is an example of discrete data?

options.a: Number of students in a class

explanation: Discrete = counted (whole numbers). Continuous = measured (any value).

questionText: A testable hypothesis must be:
explanation: Falsifiable hypothesis = testable. Can be supported or rejected by data.

subtopic: Pilot study small scale preliminary test
questionText: What is the purpose of a pilot study?

options.a: Small-scale test to refine methods before full experiment

explanation: Pilot = small preliminary trial → identify problems, refine procedure → then run full study.

questionText: Express 0.000045 in scientific notation.
explanation: 0.000045 = 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ (move decimal 5 places right).

questionText: How many significant figures does 0.00340 have?
explanation: Leading zeros not significant. Trailing zeros after decimal are significant. So 3,4,0 = 3 sf.

questionText: The equation v² = u² + 2as. What are the dimensions of 2as?
explanation: a [m/s²] × s [m] = m²/s². So 2as has units of (m/s)² = m²/s². Velocity squared = m²/s².

questionText: A vernier caliper typically measures to a precision of:
explanation: Vernier caliper = 0.01 cm precision (micrometer screw gauge = 0.001 cm / 0.01 mm).

questionText: A micrometer screw gauge typically measures to a precision of:
explanation: Micrometer = 0.01 mm precision (more precise than vernier 0.1 mm).

questionText: A stopwatch typically measures to 0.01 s. What event has duration in this range?
explanation: 100 m race ≈ 10-13 s; stopwatch 0.01 s reads 10.23 s. Earth rotation too long; light too fast.

questionText: Convert 5 km/h to m/s.
If a 50 cm measurement has 0.5 cm uncertainty, the percentage error is:
explanation: % error = (uncertainty / measured value) × 100 = (0.5 / 50) × 100 = 1%.

questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes distance from displacement?

options.a: Distance is a scalar; displacement is a vector

explanation: Distance = total path length (scalar). Displacement = net change in position (vector).

questionText: Which of these is a physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction (i.e., a vector)?
explanation: Vector = magnitude + direction. Velocity has both. Speed is magnitude only.

topic: Chemistry - Acids, Bases and Salts Advanced
questionText: Why does an antacid tablet relieve heartburn?
explanation: Antacid = weak base (Mg(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃); neutralises HCl in stomach → raises pH → relief.

topic: Chemistry - Acids, Bases and Salts Advanced
subtopic: Brine electrolysis product soap making NaOH
questionText: In the chlor-alkali process, NaOH is produced because:

options.a: OH⁻ remains after H⁺ discharged at cathode (and Cl⁻ at anode)

explanation: Na⁺ + OH⁻ remain in solution (after H₂ + Cl₂ released) → NaOH solution for soap making etc.

topic: Chemistry - Acids, Bases and Salts Advanced
subtopic: Litmus natural indicator lichen plant source
questionText: Litmus paper is made from:
explanation: Litmus = vegetable dye from lichens (e.g., Roccella tinctoria) + absorbed on paper.

topic: Chemistry - Acids, Bases and Salts Advanced
questionText: What is concentration of a solution with 0.5 mol of solute in 2 dm³ of solution?
explanation: M = moles / volume = 0.5 / 2 = 0.25 mol/dm³.

topic: Chemistry - Acids, Bases and Salts Advanced
subtopic: Weak base ammonia example typical reaction
questionText: Ammonia (NH₃) is an example of:
explanation: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ (partial ionisation) = weak base.

questionText: An ionic bond typically forms when electronegativity difference exceeds:
explanation: ΔEN > 1.7 → ionic bond (large difference).

questionText: A polar molecule has:
explanation: Polar molecule = permanent net dipole due to polar bonds + shape not cancelling dipoles.

questionText: Why are ionic solids brittle (shatter when struck)?

options.a: Layer shift brings like charges together → repulsion cracks crystal

explanation: Ionic lattice: applied force shifts layers → same-sign ions adjacent → strong repulsion → shatter.

subtopic: Van der Waals forces dependence molecular size
questionText: Van der Waals forces are stronger in molecules that:
explanation: More electrons = more polarisable → stronger temporary dipole → stronger London forces.

questionText: Why is a metal both a good conductor of electricity AND malleable?

options.a: Delocalised electrons allow movement and layer shifting

explanation: Metallic bonding: delocalised e⁻ (mobile, carry current) + layers slide (malleability).

questionText: Absolute zero is the temperature at which:
explanation: 0 K = −273.15°C = theoretical lowest T (no molecular motion, Third Law of Thermodynamics).

questionText: How does CO₂ in the atmosphere contribute to the greenhouse effect?

options.a: Absorbs infrared radiation emitted from Earth surface

explanation: CO₂ absorbs IR radiation from warmed Earth → traps heat → global warming.

subtopic: Land breeze night time direction ocean
questionText: At night, the land breeze blows from:
explanation: Night: land cools faster than sea → cool land air sinks → warmer sea air rises → breeze from land to sea.

subtopic: Specific heat capacity water high reason
questionText: Why does water have a high specific heat capacity?

options.a: Hydrogen bonds require extra energy to break

explanation: H-bonds need extra energy to break/move → water absorbs lots of heat per °C rise.

subtopic: Convection cannot occur in vacuum why
questionText: Convection cannot occur in a vacuum because:
explanation: Convection requires fluid movement. Vacuum = no medium = no convection.

questionText: What are the two most abundant gases in Earth's atmosphere?
explanation: Dry air: ~78% N₂, ~21% O₂, ~1% Ar + trace CO₂, etc.

subtopic: Moon phases new full quarter lunar cycle
questionText: How long does the Moon take for one cycle of phases (new moon to new moon)?
explanation: Synodic month (new → new) ≈ 29.5 days = lunar cycle.

subtopic: Sun star classification main sequence colour
questionText: The Sun is classified as which colour/type on H-R diagram?
explanation: Sun = G2V yellow main sequence star (yellow dwarf).

questionText: GPS satellites orbit Earth primarily to provide:
explanation: GPS = 24+ MEO satellites; triangulate Earth positions for navigation (mobile phones, planes).

questionText: Astronomers measure the distance to nearby stars by:
explanation: Stellar parallax = apparent shift due to Earth's orbit → calculate distance (triangulation).

questionText: An object falls freely from rest for 3 seconds. Find its velocity at that instant. #001
explanation: In free fall under gravity (g ~ 10 m/s^2), velocity after 3 s: v = g x t = 10 x 3 = 30 m/s.

questionText: A current of 5 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. Find the voltage across it. #002
explanation: V = I x R = 5 x 10 = 50 V. (Verified against KSSM Form 4 Physics standard formula.)

questionText: Which of the following correctly describes Archimedes' principle? #003

options.a: A liquid in a connected vessel rises to the same level
options.b: Pressure in a fluid increases linearly with depth
options.c: An object immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced
options.d: An object's mass equals its volume times its density

explanation: Archimedes' principle: a body submerged in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.

questionText: A wave has frequency 500 Hz. What is its period? #004
Under what conditions does total internal reflection occur? #005

options.a: When light travels from a less dense medium to a denser medium
options.b: Only when light passes through a thin film
options.c: Only when light is reflected from a mirror
options.d: When light travels from a denser medium to a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle

explanation: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser medium (higher refractive index) to a less dense medium (lower refractive index) at an angle greater than the critical angle, causing the light to be completely reflected back into the denser medium.

questionText: A converging lens forms an image of an object placed 40 cm away at a distance of 40 cm. Find the focal length of the lens. #006
How much heat is needed to raise 2 kg of water (c = 4200 J/kgK) by 30 °C? #007
An appliance operates at 12 V and draws 2 A. What is its power rating? #008
explanation: Power P = V x I = 12 x 2 = 24 W.

questionText: Convert 25 km to m. #009
An appliance operates at 24 V and draws 2 A. What is its power rating? #010
explanation: Power P = V x I = 24 x 2 = 48 W.

questionText: An object travels 200 m in 5 seconds. Calculate its speed. #011
explanation: Speed = distance / time = 200 / 5 = 40 m/s.

questionText: What is the basic function of a semiconductor diode? #331

options.b: Pairs of atoms sharing electrons equally

questionText: What type of bond forms between two hydrogen atoms in H2? #136

options.b: Ionic bond (transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal)
options.c: Hydrogen bond (weak bond between H and N/O/F)
options.d: Covalent bond (sharing of electrons between non-metals)

explanation: Ionic bonds form by complete transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, producing positive and negative ions held together by electrostatic attraction (e.g., NaCl from Na + Cl).

options.d: Enzymes are consumed during reactions and provide energy

explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts (typically globular proteins) that speed up biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy. They are NOT consumed in the reaction and are highly specific (lock-and-key / induced fit models).

questionText: Which of the following correctly defines a balanced diet? #396

options.a: A balanced diet contains only proteins
options.b: A balanced diet contains the correct amounts of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water
options.c: A balanced diet is the same for everyone

explanation: A balanced diet provides the correct proportions of macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) and micronutrients (vitamins, minerals), plus water and dietary fibre, for healthy body function.

questionText: How does the human heart separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood? #397

options.b: Right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body

explanation: The human heart has four chambers. Right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from body -> right ventricle pumps it to the lungs via pulmonary artery. Left atrium receives oxygenated blood from lungs -> left ventricle pumps it to the body via aorta.

questionText: Active transport requires #398

options.b: Energy (ATP) and carrier proteins; moves substances against concentration gradient
options.d: No energy; moves substances down the concentration gradient

explanation: Energy (ATP) and carrier proteins; moves substances against concentration gradient — standard KSSM T4 membrane transport principle.

questionText: Which of the following correctly defines transpiration in plants? #399

options.a: Transpiration is the transport of sugars
options.b: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves (mainly through stomata)
options.c: Transpiration is the absorption of water by roots
options.d: Transpiration is the loss of oxygen from leaves

explanation: Transpiration: the loss of water vapour from plants, mainly through tiny pores (stomata) on the leaf surface. It creates a transpiration pull that helps draw water up from the roots through the xylem.

questionText: What is the function of the chloroplast in a cell? #400

options.a: Site of photosynthesis in plant cells; contains chlorophyll
options.b: Produces ATP energy through aerobic respiration
options.c: Synthesises proteins from amino acids using mRNA
options.d: Stores genetic material (DNA) and controls cell activities

explanation: Chloroplast: Site of photosynthesis in plant cells; contains chlorophyll. Other organelles have different roles in eukaryotic cells.

questionText: Which of the following correctly distinguishes xylem from phloem? #401

options.a: Both xylem and phloem transport only water
options.b: Phloem transports water; xylem transports food
options.c: Xylem transports water and minerals from roots to leaves; phloem transports organic food (sucrose) from leaves to other parts
options.d: Both xylem and phloem transport only food

explanation: Xylem: vascular tissue that transports water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves (one-way flow, transpiration-driven). Phloem: vascular tissue that transports organic food (mainly sucrose) from leaves to other parts of the plant (two-way, translocation).

questionText: Which of the following correctly distinguishes xylem from phloem? #482

questionText: Which of the following correctly describes the body's defence mechanisms? #486
